query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated-temperature exposure to either oxidizing or reducing gases promotes selective oxidation at the grain boundaries of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, leading to local depletion of critical elements (notably Cr and Ti) that normally contribute to cohesion. This internal oxidation process facilitates the formation of brittle phases or weakened interfaces along the grain boundaries, which in turn act as sites for crack nucleation and growth under stress, eventually triggering catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous FCC matrix and uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Controlled exposure of the alloy to elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–1000 °C) in either oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen-enriched atmosphere) or reducing (e.g., hydrogen-rich atmosphere) environments for varied durations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (700–1000 °C), controlled gas atmosphere (oxidizing vs. reducing), with and without simultaneous mechanical loading to probe stress-enhanced effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries of the FCC matrix, along which selective oxidation and potential brittle phase precipitation occur.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature exposure, the limited content of protective elements (Cr, Ti) is preferentially oxidized at grain boundaries. This selective oxidation leads to elemental depletion and consequent loss of grain boundary cohesion, promoting brittle phase formation. The weakened interfaces then serve as initiation sites for intergranular cracking when the alloy is subjected to mechanical stress, resulting in catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pristine state, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will develop discontinuous or non-protective oxide scales at the grain boundaries, accompanied by measurable depletion of Cr and Ti and reduced ductility and fracture toughness. Under reducing conditions, a lack of stable protective oxides may lead instead to rapid internal dealloying and similar embrittlement, both of which are observable as inferior mechanical performance and earlier crack initiation.
generation.baseline: Untreated additively manufactured alloy exhibiting a homogeneous FCC grain structure with established mechanical strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature conditions (700–1000 °C) with defined oxidizing or reducing atmospheres; deviations from these exposure limits may invoke different degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of grain-boundary oxidation and the critical levels of elemental depletion required to trigger brittle phase precipitation are not yet quantified. The interplay between oxidation kinetics, microstructural evolution, and mechanical load is also somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens. Subject one set to high-temperature exposure (e.g., 800 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere and a second set in a reducing atmosphere for increasing durations (e.g., 50, 100, 200 hours). A control set will be maintained in an inert environment. After exposure, conduct detailed microstructural analyses (via SEM/TEM with EDS) to assess grain boundary composition and oxide distribution as well as mechanical tests (tensile and fracture toughness) to evaluate degradation.
measurements: Phase and oxide scale identification (XRD, TEM)
Mechanical property changes (tensile strength, ductility, fracture toughness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If exposed samples do not exhibit significant grain boundary depletion of Cr and Ti, do not form detectable brittle oxide or secondary phases at the grain boundaries, and maintain mechanical performance comparable to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis that selective intergranular oxidation drives degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
